title: Sweet or Dry? How to Read the Sake Meter Value
description: Learn how the Sake Meter Value relates to sweetness and dryness, and why acidity matters when judging flavor.
bodyHtml:
You will often see the term "Sake Meter Value" on sake labels and in product descriptions. You may have heard that positive values indicate dryness and negative values indicate sweetness, but the numbers themselves can still be difficult to interpret.

What does the Sake Meter Value measure?

The Sake Meter Value expresses the amount of sugar dissolved in sake as a number, with water set as the reference point of 0. More sugar makes the liquid denser and moves the value toward the negative side. Less sugar brings its density closer to that of water and moves the value toward the positive side. In general, a higher positive value suggests a drier sake, while a larger negative value suggests a sweeter one.

As a general guide, +6 or above is often described as "very dry," +3 to +6 as "dry," around -1 to +2 as "medium," and -3 or below as "sweet." These ranges are only a guide.

The number alone does not determine flavor

It is too simple to decide that a sake is sweet or dry from the Sake Meter Value alone. Even at the same value, the impression on the palate can vary greatly depending on acidity, alcohol content, and the way its aroma presents itself. Higher acidity can give the finish a crisp edge, making a sake feel drier even when it contains more sugar.

Our sake detail pages show the Sake Meter Value alongside acidity, as well as flavor scales for "sweet to dry" and "light to rich." Looking at both the figures and the sensory descriptions makes it easier to imagine how the sake may taste.

See how it works with actual bottles

For example, Hakkaisan Tokubetsu Honjozo is a dry style with a Sake Meter Value of around +4, known for a light, clean profile. By contrast, another dry sake such as Kariho Yamahai Junmai Chokarakuchi also has acidity and body. Even within the broad category of "dry," sake can show many different expressions.

If you are not yet sure whether you prefer sweet or dry sake, answer a few questions in our one-minute quiz to find a style close to your preferences. If you would rather browse by aroma and flavor profile, try the Sou (light and crisp) or Jun (rich and full-bodied) pages.

title: Junmai, Ginjo, and Daiginjo: A Simple Guide
description: A clear guide to sake classifications such as junmai, ginjo, and daiginjo, based on ingredients and rice polishing ratio.
bodyHtml:
Sake labels are filled with terms such as "Junmai Daiginjo" and "Honjozo" that may be unfamiliar at first. These are classifications known as designated grades, determined mainly by the ingredients and the rice polishing ratio (how much of the rice is polished away).

First, two groups based on ingredients

Broadly speaking, sake falls into two groups. Junmai styles are made only from rice, rice koji, and water. Non-junmai styles, including honjozo, also contain a small amount of brewer's alcohol. Brewer's alcohol can lighten the flavor and lift the aroma; its use does not mean the sake is of lower quality.

How the rice polishing ratio changes the classification

The rice polishing ratio is the percentage of each brown rice grain that remains after polishing. A lower number means more of the outer portion of the grain, which can contribute less desirable flavors, has been removed.

  • Junmai: No prescribed rice polishing ratio. Many examples emphasize the savory character of rice.
  • Junmai Ginjo: Rice polishing ratio of 60% or less. More likely to develop a fragrant ginjo aroma.
  • Junmai Daiginjo: Rice polishing ratio of 50% or less. Often aromatic, delicate, and low in distracting flavors.
  • Honjozo: Rice polishing ratio of 70% or less, with brewer's alcohol added. Typically offers a clean drinking profile.

Dassai Junmai Daiginjo 23, for example, is polished to 23%, just as its name suggests. Removing 77% of the outer grain gives it a clear aroma and flavor with few distracting notes.

Choose between aroma and rice-driven savoriness

Sake with a lower polishing ratio, meaning a smaller number, tends to fall into the aromatic Kaori style. Junmai made with a higher polishing ratio, meaning less of the grain is removed, is more likely to have the pronounced rice character associated with the Jun style. Neither is inherently better: choosing according to your mood or meal is part of the pleasure of sake.

Once you understand these classifications, continue with our guide to reading a sake label.

title: 10 Approachable Sakes for Beginners
description: Ten approachable sakes for newcomers, organized by flavor profile, region, and price range to make choosing a bottle easier.
bodyHtml:
We selected ten gentle, approachable bottles that can be enjoyable even if you feel that sake may not be for you. All are distributed nationwide in Japan and are relatively easy to find at accessible prices.

For a clean, crisp style

  • Hakkaisan Tokubetsu Honjozo (Niigata) — A classic light, dry style with little heaviness that pairs easily with food.
  • Ichinokura Mukansa Honjozo Karakuchi (Miyagi) — A light, crisp staple for an everyday evening drink.
  • Jokigen Yamahai Junmai (Ishikawa) — The richness associated with yamahai in an approachable profile.

For a fragrant, easy-drinking style

  • Dewazakura Oka Ginjo (Yamagata) — Well regarded as an introduction to fruity ginjo aromas.
  • Asabiraki Junmai Ginjo White Label (Iwate) — A gentle aroma and soft entry on the palate.
  • Hijiri Junmai Ginjo Yamada Nishiki 50 (Gunma) — An accessible way to enjoy the refined aroma associated with Yamada Nishiki.

For a gentle taste of rice

  • Nanbu Bijin Tokubetsu Junmai (Iwate) — Well-balanced savoriness and a clean finish.
  • KID Junmai (Wakayama) — A friendly, balanced bottle suited to everyday occasions.
  • Sentoku Junmai (Miyazaki) — Tropical aromas lend it a lighter sake character.

For a small indulgence

  • Kunimare Daiginjo (Hokkaido) — Daiginjo's fragrant character at an accessible price.

If you are unsure where to begin, use our one-minute quiz to identify a style before choosing. To browse more deliberately, visit the Sou or Jun category pages.

title: How to Choose Sake for Sashimi
description: Learn how to pair sake with sashimi by considering aroma intensity and the richness or fat content of the fish.
bodyHtml:
Sashimi is one of the foods most often discussed alongside sake. Matching the style of sake to the type of fish and its fat content can make the meal feel more harmonious.

Choose a clean style for white or lean fish

Delicate white fish such as sea bream and flounder pair well with a Sou style whose aroma is not too pronounced, or a light Kaori style. The key is to keep the sake's aroma from overwhelming the fish's subtle savoriness.

Choose a richer style for fattier fish

For fatty fish such as tuna belly or yellowtail, a Jun style with some body and savoriness can stand up to the richness and bring the flavors together. Junmai with firm acidity can also work well.

Example pairings

A fragrant daiginjo such as Otokoyama Junmai Daiginjo, for example, is considered a good match for delicate white-fish sashimi. A full-bodied junmai such as Tengumai Yamahai Junmai, on the other hand, pairs well with fattier fish or zuke sashimi seasoned with a robust soy-based marinade.

To find sake by dishes beyond sashimi, see our list of sake for sashimi and sushi. The pages for yakitori and meat dishes and cheese and snacks may also be useful.

title: How to Store Sake Properly
description: Practical guidance on storage temperature, protection from light and vibration, and handling sake after opening.
bodyHtml:
Even a delicious sake can lose its character if stored incorrectly. Here are the basic steps you can take at home to preserve it.

A cool, dark place is the basic rule

Sake is sensitive to ultraviolet light and high temperatures. Avoid direct sunlight and places with large temperature swings, and keep it refrigerated whenever possible. Nama sake and nama genshu deteriorate particularly quickly and must be stored in the refrigerator.

Store bottles upright

Unlike wine, sake does not need to be stored on its side. Prolonged contact between the liquid and a crown cap or screw cap may affect the flavor, so the general rule is to store bottles upright.

Drink it reasonably soon after opening

Once a bottle is opened, exposure to air begins oxidation and gradually changes its aroma and flavor. Keep it refrigerated and aim to finish it within about two weeks to one month. The aromatic character of a Kaori style tends to show change relatively clearly, so enjoy it sooner.

By contrast, sake made to express the changes brought by maturation, such as the Juku style, can offer the interest of developing new facets over time.

If you cannot finish the bottle

Our guide to sake shelf life and how soon to finish an opened bottle explains this topic in more detail. If you are unsure about storage, starting with a size you can finish, such as 300 ml or 720 ml, is another practical option.

title: Which Sake Works Warm? A Guide to Serving Temperatures
description: Explore traditional sake temperature terms, from well chilled to hot, and learn which flavor styles suit each range.
bodyHtml:
Sake is unusual in how dramatically its aroma and flavor can change with temperature. It can be enjoyed both chilled and warmed, so let us look at that versatility across the main temperature ranges.

Names for each temperature range

  • Yuki-hie (around 5°C) and hana-hie (around 10°C): Well-chilled temperatures that suit the fragrant Kaori style.
  • Suzu-hie (around 15°C) and room temperature (around 20°C): Temperatures that make it easier to balance aroma and savoriness, suited to the Sou style.
  • Nuru-kan (around 40°C): A temperature that brings out the savoriness of rice and works well with the Jun style.
  • Atsu-kan (around 50°C): A temperature that makes aroma rise strongly, suited to the Juku style and full-bodied honjozo or junmai.

Characteristics of sake that improves when warmed

Junmai and honjozo with firm acidity or body are generally suited to warming. With a kimoto sake such as Daishichi Junmai Kimoto, warming expands the rice-derived savoriness and highlights its mellow profile. Yamahai sake such as Tengumai Yamahai Junmai is likewise considered well suited to temperatures from nuru-kan to atsu-kan.

Sake whose strengths may be less apparent when warmed

Conversely, aromatic and delicate styles such as daiginjo and junmai daiginjo are generally served chilled so their fragrance can be appreciated. Higher temperatures may cause their delicate aromas to dissipate, so begin by checking the serving recommendations on the label.

You can also check the "Recommended serving style" section on each sake detail page to see which temperature range suits a bottle you have.

title: How to Choose Sake as a Gift, by Price Range
description: A practical guide to choosing sake gifts by budget and occasion, from casual visits to important celebrations.
bodyHtml:
Sake is also popular as a gift because of its attractive presentation and the stories associated with individual bottles. Here are some points to consider at different budgets.

Up to about ¥3,000: A casual gift

Even at an everyday price, a bottle with a sense of regional character can make a welcome gift. Otokoyama Junmai Daiginjo, for example, offers the fragrant character of junmai daiginjo at an accessible price.

About ¥3,000–¥5,000: Seasonal greetings and anniversaries

This is a standard range for a slightly more formal gift, such as a midsummer or year-end gift for someone who has helped you. A well-known label such as Kubota Manju Junmai Daiginjo can be a reassuring choice.

¥5,000 and above: Special anniversaries and celebrations

For a wedding, milestone birthday, or another important occasion, consider a rarer bottle. Labels such as Kokuryu Ishidaya and Dassai Junmai Daiginjo 23 are especially popular as gifts because their names convey a sense of occasion.

You can also choose according to the occasion

Budget is not the only guide. You can also think about when and how you would like the recipient to enjoy it. Our gift sake list brings together bottles suited to giving, while the special-occasion list may help when choosing a bottle for a celebratory toast.

title: Sake vs. Wine: What Beginners Should Know
description: Compare sake and wine through their ingredients, production methods, aromas, serving temperatures, and pairing styles.
bodyHtml:
"How is sake different from wine?" is a common question among people beginning to explore sake. Here are the main differences.

Different ingredients: Rice vs. grapes

The most fundamental difference is the main ingredient. Wine is made by fermenting the sugar naturally present in grapes. In sake, koji converts the starch in rice into sugar, which is then fermented. This process, called multiple parallel fermentation, is rare on a global scale. It also contributes to sake's distinctive rice-derived savoriness, or umami.

Types of aroma

While wine aromas originate in fruit, sake's fragrant ginjo aromas come from aromatic compounds produced by yeast during fermentation. A fruity Kaori style is sometimes described as approachable in a way similar to white wine.

Temperature changes the experience

Wine is also served chilled or at room temperature, but sake stands out for the exceptionally broad range at which it can be enjoyed, from yuki-hie to atsu-kan. Our guide to warmed sake explains these temperatures in more detail.

Sake and wine share some selection cues

Both wine and sake can be chosen to accompany food, and both range gradually from light to rich. Wine drinkers approaching sake might begin with a fragrant Kaori style or a crisp Sou style, which may feel more familiar and accessible. If you do not yet know your preference, try our one-minute quiz.

title: Sake Shelf Life and How Soon to Finish an Open Bottle
description: Why sake labels often omit a best-before date, plus practical guidance for unopened and opened bottles.
bodyHtml:
Look closely at a sake label and you may notice a production date rather than a best-before date. There is a clear reason for this.

Why sake has no best-before date

Sake has a relatively high alcohol content of around 15%, which makes it resistant to spoilage. Under Japan's food-labeling rules, it therefore does not require a best-before date, and labels generally show the production date, meaning when the brewery bottled it. This does not mean that its quality will remain unchanged indefinitely.

A guide for unopened bottles

If an unopened bottle is kept in a cool, dark place, it is generally considered to remain relatively stable and enjoyable for about six months to one year after production. Nama sake and nama genshu deteriorate more quickly, however, so drink them sooner and always keep them refrigerated. Our guide to proper sake storage provides more detail.

A guide after opening

Opening the bottle begins oxidation. Keep it refrigerated and aim to finish it within about two weeks to one month. A smaller 300 ml bottle is easier to finish before flavor changes become noticeable.

You can also appreciate change over time

Not every sake is meant to be consumed as soon as possible. Some, including the Juku style, are made so that changes in aroma over time become part of the experience. Start with the label or a bottle description such as the one for Kokuryu Ishidaya, and find the approach that suits that sake.

title: How to Read a Sake Label: Essential Terms
description: Understand common sake-label terms including rice polishing ratio, brewing rice, Sake Meter Value, acidity, and alcohol.
bodyHtml:
A sake label contains a wealth of information that can help you choose a bottle. Once you understand the terminology, the label alone can give you a general idea of how the sake may taste.

Designated grade (Junmai Daiginjo, Honjozo, and others)

This classification is determined by the ingredients and rice polishing ratio. See our guide to the differences among junmai, ginjo, and daiginjo for details.

Rice polishing ratio

This number indicates how much the brown rice has been polished. A lower number means more has been removed and generally makes fragrant aromas more likely to develop. Dassai Junmai Daiginjo 23, for example, has a polishing ratio of 23%, meaning 77% of each grain is removed.

Rice variety (sake rice)

Sake is often made with varieties developed for brewing, such as Yamada Nishiki, Gohyakumangoku, and Omachi. Even within the same designated grade, the rice variety can change the impression of the flavor.

Sake Meter Value and acidity

These figures provide a guide to sweetness and dryness. Our Sake Meter Value guide explains them in more detail.

Alcohol content

Typical sake is around 15–16% alcohol, although lower-alcohol styles at around 12–13% have become more common in recent years. This is another useful figure to check when you want something lighter.

Production terms such as nama and kimoto

Nama sake is not heat-pasteurized at any stage and is known for its fresh aroma. Kimoto refers to a traditional method of preparing the yeast starter, allowing lactic acid to develop naturally instead of adding it. Some bottles state these methods on their labels or packaging, including Daishichi Junmai Kimoto and Tengumai Yamahai Junmai.

Once the terms begin to feel familiar, browse the sake catalog and compare labels. Choosing sake becomes much more enjoyable when you know what to look for.

title: Kimoto and Yamahai: A Simple Guide to Traditional Sake Starters
description: Learn what kimoto and yamahai share, how the yama-oroshi step separates them, and what to check when choosing a bottle.
bodyHtml:
You may see the terms "kimoto" and "yamahai" on sake labels. Both refer to traditional ways of preparing the yeast starter, but their names alone do not make the difference obvious. The easiest place to begin is with what they share.

Both belong to the kimoto family of yeast starters

The yeast starter creates the foundation in which the yeast used to ferment the main mash is cultivated. Unlike the sokujomoto approach, in which prepared lactic acid is added during production, kimoto and yamahai establish conditions in which lactic acid is produced through the activity of lactic-acid bacteria. For this reason, both are grouped as kimoto-family starters.

The difference is whether yama-oroshi is performed

Kimoto includes a step called yama-oroshi, in which steamed rice, koji, and water are worked together with paddles. Yamahai is short for yama-oroshi haishi moto, meaning a starter that omits this step. Yamahai is therefore not unrelated to kimoto. It is easier to understand it as a revised process that retains the basic approach of a kimoto-family starter while dispensing with yama-oroshi.

Do not predict flavor from the method alone

Kimoto and yamahai bottles are sometimes introduced as styles with noticeable acidity and rice-driven savoriness. The actual impression, however, also varies with the rice, polishing ratio, Sake Meter Value, acidity, maturation, and serving temperature. Rather than assuming every yamahai will taste heavy, check the data for the individual bottle. Many examples in this catalog can be found under the Jun style.

Compare the methods through individual bottles

One kimoto example is Daishichi Junmai Kimoto, for which room temperature and nuru-kan are recommended. Yamahai examples include Tengumai Yamahai Junmai, whose catalog data emphasizes acidity and savoriness, and Kariho Yamahai Junmai Chokarakuchi, with a Sake Meter Value of +12. Comparing them shows the range that exists even within related production methods.

Trying small pours at room temperature and nuru-kan is one way to compare changes in aroma, acidity, and savoriness. See our guide to warmed sake for the main temperature terms and warming basics.

title: Why Cheese and Sake Can Work Together
description: A practical introduction to pairing cheese and sake by comparing aroma, flavor intensity, acidity, and serving temperature.
bodyHtml:
Japanese food may be the first thing that comes to mind when choosing something to serve with sake, but this catalog includes many bottles with cheese and snacks among their pairing suggestions. Instead of beginning with rigid rules, start by matching the intensity of the aromas and flavors.

Begin with a gentle combination

With a cheese whose aroma and saltiness are restrained, a light, aromatic sake makes it easier to compare the character of each. Browse the sake for cheese and snacks page for candidates. If fragrance is your main reference point, the Kaori style is another useful place to look.

For a stronger cheese, check the sake's structure

If the cheese seems more pronounced in aroma or saltiness, also look at the sake's acidity, savoriness, and sharpness. The catalog entry for Suigei Junmai Ginjo Ginrei, for example, records a fresh citrus-like aroma, clear acidity, and a crisp finish, and includes cheese among its pairing suggestions. Try a small amount of each and check whether the aroma or flavor of either one remains disproportionately strong.

Choose by the impression of aroma and sweetness

Gekkeikan Horin Junmai Daiginjo is recorded with a Muscat-like aroma and refined sweetness. Dassai Junmai Daiginjo 23 is described with a fragrant aroma, honey-like sweetness, and a long, crisp finish. Cheese is listed for both bottles, but the result will vary with the type and amount of cheese, so comparing small portions is practical.

Adjust the temperature and amount

Every bottle mentioned here includes yuki-hie or hana-hie among its recommended temperatures. Begin with the sake chilled. If its aroma seems closed, allow the temperature to rise slightly. Alternating small tastes of cheese and sake, rather than taking a large amount at once, makes differences between combinations easier to notice.
